title: Vara as agent-as-recall
dek: A grounded recall layer gives an agent useful memory without letting it treat every old note as truth.
body:
I have plenty of notes. The harder problem is getting an agent to recall the right note, show where the answer came from, and stop when the evidence runs out.

Vara is my first attempt to make that boundary explicit. It is a dedicated recall agent over the material I have already chosen to keep: bookmark summaries, specifications, long-term memory, and selected daily notes. Before Vara answers, it reads a maintained catalogue of those sources. It can open only the entries listed there, and every answer cites the source it used.

## Memory is not the same as recall

Raw memory is useful because it preserves context. It is also messy. Notes repeat themselves, decisions change, and a sentence written during an early idea can look authoritative months later. Giving an agent unrestricted access to all of that material does not create reliable recall. It gives the model a larger pile to interpret.

The catalogue adds a deliberate layer between storage and an answer. Each entry records what a source is, where it lives, and a short description of what it contains. Vara uses that catalogue to decide which material is relevant, then reads the original source before responding. The catalogue points; the source proves.

That distinction matters when two notes disagree. Vara should not smooth the conflict into a confident summary. It should cite both and describe the disagreement. If the catalogue has nothing that supports the question, the correct answer is that the indexed material does not contain it.

## A small boundary I can inspect

The first version is intentionally plain. The catalogue and its operating log are readable documents. New supported material is added incrementally. Queries and link checks leave dated records. A daily check reports references that no longer resolve, but it does not silently delete them.

There is no generated second brain hiding behind the agent. Vara does not rewrite the source material into topic pages, and it does not turn a plausible association into a citation. The original notes remain the source of truth.

This makes failures easier to diagnose. If an answer is weak, I can ask whether the right source was catalogued, whether the catalogue described it clearly, and whether Vara followed the citation boundary. Those are concrete failure modes. “The model forgot” is not.

## What shipped

Vara now runs as a dedicated agent with the grounded recall rule built into its workflow. Existing material was catalogued for the first use, and new bookmark summaries and specifications can join the catalogue as they move through their normal workflows. The recall path has been tested against real sources, including answers that cite the exact documents used. A scheduled link check verifies the catalogue each day.

The delivery also passed its final human QA gate. That matters here because the interesting claim is not that a model can summarise notes. It is that the system can keep the model inside a visible evidence boundary.

The next questions are operational. Which notes are worth admitting to the catalogue? How much description is enough to find a source without biasing the answer? When old sources conflict, should the catalogue carry stronger status signals? I want to answer those from real recall work before adding search infrastructure or more abstraction.

For now, Vara has a narrow job: find what I have chosen to remember, cite it exactly, and say when it cannot support an answer.
